entry: American animator, filmmaker, songwriter and actor. With [[Trey Parker]], whom he met at the University of Colorado Boulder, he created the animated satire *South Park* (since 1997) and the films *South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut* (1999) and *Team America: World Police* (2004). With Robert Lopez, Stone co-created the musical *The Book of Mormon* (2011). He has won five Primetime Emmy Awards and a Peabody for *South Park*, and three Tony Awards and a Grammy Award for *The Book of Mormon*. In 2026 he was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame.

Peak in the [[Alps]] on the border between [[Switzerland]] and Italy. Its summit, 4,478 m (14,692 ft) above sea level, is one of the highest in the Alps and [[Europe]]. It has been claimed to be the most photographed mountain in the world, and it is an emblem of Switzerland. The first ascent, in 1865, ended in a fall that killed four of the seven climbers. The north face was not climbed until 1931. Over 500 alpinists are estimated to have died on the mountain, one of the deadliest peaks in the world.

American actor. He gained attention in the coming-of-age comedy *Dazed and Confused* (1993) and became a leading man with *A Time to Kill* (1996). Romantic comedies in the 2000s made him a [[Sex symbol|sex symbol]]. His portrayal of Ron Woodroof, a cowboy diagnosed with AIDS, in *Dallas Buyers Club* (2013) won him the Academy Award for Best Actor. He starred as Rust Cohle in the first season of [[HBO]]'s *True Detective* (2014), earning a Primetime Emmy nomination. Later films include *Interstellar* (2014) and *The Gentlemen* (2019).

Canadian and American actor. He was best known for playing Chandler Bing on the [[NBC]] sitcom *Friends* (1994–2004), for which he received a Primetime Emmy nomination in 2002. He also starred in *Mr. Sunshine* (2011) and *Go On* (2012), and in films including *The Whole Nine Yards* (2000). He struggled with addiction to drugs and alcohol for most of his life. He became an advocate for addiction treatment and received the Champion of Recovery Award from the [[White House]] Office of National Drug Control Policy in 2013. He died from the acute effects of [[Ketamine|ketamine]], with accidental drowning as a contributing factor.

Student at the University of Wyoming whose murder drew national attention to hate crime legislation. Shepard was beaten, tortured and left to die near Laramie, Wyoming, in October 1998, and died six days later. Aaron McKinney and Russell Henderson each received two consecutive life sentences. The prosecutor argued that the killing was premeditated and driven by greed. Media coverage focused on Shepard's sexual orientation as a possible motive, while some investigative reporting has attributed the attack to a failed drug robbery. The Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, signed by [[Barack Obama]] in 2009, is named in part for him.

King of [[Kingdom of Hungary|Hungary]] and Croatia (r. 1458–1490). Son of the regent [[John Hunyadi]], he was proclaimed king at age 14 after his uncle Michael Szilágyi persuaded the Estates to elect him; he took effective control within two weeks. He was elected King of [[Bohemia]] in 1469 and adopted the title Duke of Austria in 1487. He fought the Czech mercenaries who dominated Upper Hungary and the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III, occupying Lower Austria between 1482 and 1487. He briefly attacked [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]]-held territory but gave up his anti-Ottoman policy after receiving no substantial aid from Christian powers. He established the Black Army of Hungary, one of the earliest professional standing armies of medieval Europe, reformed the administration of justice, and reduced the power of the barons. His royal library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana, was one of the largest book collections in Europe. With his patronage, Hungary became the first country to embrace the [[Renaissance]] from Italy. He remains a folk hero, Matthias the Just, in Hungarian and Slovak tales.

Disciple of the Buddha, one of his two foremost male disciples. Born Kolita, Maudgalyāyana and [[Śāriputra]] became spiritual wanderers in their youth, encountered the Buddha's teaching and ordained as monks; Maudgalyāyana attained enlightenment shortly after. He is depicted in Buddhist art accompanying the Buddha, and he was known for the psychic powers he used in teaching. In many early Buddhist canons he helped reunite the monastic community after Devadatta caused a [[Schism|schism]]. He died at age 84, killed through the efforts of a rival sect; scriptures describe this as the karmic result of having killed his parents in a previous life. Post-canonical texts describe him transferring merit to his mother, a story behind the ghost festival observed in many Buddhist countries. He was traditionally associated with meditation and the Dharmaguptaka school. Relics attributed to him, found in the nineteenth century, are widely venerated.

Second-largest island in the [[Hawaiian Islands|Hawaiian archipelago]] (pop., 2020: 168,307). Maui covers 1,883 sq km (727.2 sq mi) and is one of Maui County's four sizable islands. Two volcanoes dominate it, Haleakalā in the southeast and the West Maui Mountains in the northwest, joined by an isthmus that gives the island its nickname, the Valley Isle. Tourism is central to the economy, with nearly three million visitors in 2022. In 2023 fire mostly destroyed the historic town of Lāhainā.

Dormant [[Shield volcano|shield volcano]] on the island of Hawaiʻi. Its summit, at 13,803 ft (4,207.3 m) above sea level, is the highest point in Hawaii. Measured from the ocean floor, its prominence of 30,610 ft (9,330 m) is rivaled only by [[Mount Everest]], and some authorities have called it the tallest mountain in the world. The volcano is about one million years old and last erupted 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. Since an access road was built in 1964, thirteen telescopes funded by eleven countries have been built at the summit, forming the [[Maunakea Observatories]], the largest such facility in the world.

A [[Shield volcano|shield volcano]] with gentle slopes, one of five volcanoes that form the island of Hawaiʻi. It is Earth's largest active volcano by mass and volume, with an estimated volume of 18,000 cubic miles (75,000 km³). Its peak is about 125 ft (38 m) lower than that of its neighbor, [[Mauna Kea]]. Its silica-poor lava is very fluid, and its eruptions tend to be non-explosive. The volcano has likely been erupting for at least 700,000 years. Its most recent eruption, from November 27 to December 13, 2022, was the first since 1984. Eruptions in 1926 and 1950 destroyed villages, and part of Hilo is built on late-19th-century lava flows. Monitored by the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory since 1912, Mauna Loa is part of the Decade Volcanoes program, which studies the world's most dangerous volcanoes. The Mauna Loa Observatory, near the summit, measures atmospheric conditions.

Group of astronomical observatories at the summit of [[Mauna Kea]] on Hawaiʻi. The facilities are independent research sites in a 525-acre (212 ha) special land use zone, the Astronomy Precinct, within the Mauna Kea Science Reserve. The precinct was established in 1967. The summit's dark skies, low [[Humidity|humidity]], low atmospheric turbulence and high elevation make it nearly ideal for astronomy. Gerard Kuiper, seeking an arid site for infrared studies, built a small telescope on Puʻu Poliʻahu, but the larger [[NASA]] project went to a University of Hawaii team led by John Jefferies. Construction of a 2.24-meter telescope began in 1967, and first light came in 1970. In 1973 [[Canada]] and [[France]] agreed to build the 3.6 m CFHT. The telescopes remain highly controversial, given the mountain's central place in Native Hawaiian religion and environmental concerns.

French composer, pianist and conductor. Often associated with Impressionism along with [[Claude Debussy]], though both composers rejected the term, Ravel was internationally regarded as France's greatest living composer in the 1920s and 1930s. His style combined clarity with modernism, baroque and neoclassical elements and, in later works, [[Jazz|jazz]]. He was renowned for orchestration; his 1922 orchestral version of Mussorgsky's *Pictures at an Exhibition* is the best known. His best-known work, *Boléro* (1928), uses repetition in place of development. A slow worker, he wrote no symphonies or church music. His works include two piano concertos, two operas and eight song cycles. He was among the first composers to recognize the potential of recording to reach a wider public.

Country in the Maghreb region of West Africa. It is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean, Western Sahara, Algeria, Mali and Senegal, and about 90% of its territory lies in the [[Sahara]]. Most of its 5.4 million people live in the south, and roughly a third live in the capital, [[Nouakchott]]. Berbers occupied the area by the 3rd century CE, and Arab tribes arriving in the late 7th century brought [[Islam]] and Arabic. [[France]] colonized the territory in the early 20th century as part of French West Africa; it became independent in 1960. Coups have recurred, including one in 2008, and the 2019 election brought what was considered the first peaceful transfer of power since independence. The economy relies mainly on agriculture and fishing. Arabic is the official language, and Islam is the state religion. The 2023 Global Slavery Index estimates that about 149,000 people are enslaved in the country.

Island country in the Indian Ocean, east of [[Madagascar]]. The republic includes the main island, Rodrigues, Agaléga and St. Brandon. Dutch settlers took possession in 1598, naming it after Maurice, Prince of Orange, and French colonization began in 1715. The [[United Kingdom]] seized the island in 1810 and held it until independence in 1968; the country became a republic in 1992 but kept the Privy Council of the United Kingdom as its highest court. Its economy long depended on sugar plantations, and the World Bank now classifies it as a high-income economy. Indo-Mauritians make up the bulk of the population, and [[Hinduism]] is the most practiced religion, the only such case in Africa. Its main island was the only known home of the [[Dodo]], which became extinct soon after human settlement. In 1965 the United Kingdom split the Chagos Archipelago away from Mauritius. The [[International Court of Justice]] has ordered its return, and a 2025 agreement recognized Mauritian sovereignty over the islands.

Iron Age empire of South Asia (c. 321–185 BCE), based in Magadha. Founded by [[Chandragupta Maurya]] around 320 BCE, it defeated the Nanda Empire and extended west to Afghanistan below the Hindu Kush and south to the northern Deccan. Its capital, Pataliputra (today Patna), lay in Magadha. Under [[Ashoka]] (c. 268–232 BCE) the empire briefly controlled most of the subcontinent except the deep south. After the Kalinga War, Ashoka embraced [[Buddhism]] and promoted its tenets in edicts across South Asia; he sponsored missionaries to Sri Lanka, northwest India and Central Asia. Roads, including the Uttarapath linking eastern Afghanistan to the capital, and coinage supported trade. The population of South Asia during the period is estimated at 15 to 30 million. In 1947 [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] proposed the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath as the State Emblem of India, and the proposal was accepted that December.

German–British theoretical physicist. Born was instrumental in developing [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. In 1925 he and [[Werner Heisenberg]] formulated its matrix mechanics representation, and the following year he proposed the now-standard interpretation of the probability density of the wave function, for which he shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics. He also contributed to [[Solid-state physics]] and [[Optics]]. At the [[University of Göttingen]], which he helped make one of the world's leading centers for physics, he supervised students including Max Delbrück, Robert Oppenheimer and Victor Weisskopf. After the [[Nazi Party]] came to power in 1933, he was suspended from his professorship because he was of Jewish descent. He emigrated to the United Kingdom, where he worked at the University of Edinburgh until 1952, and he became a British subject in 1939. His textbook *Atomic Physics* became a standard text.

German-born painter, sculptor, printmaker and poet. A pioneer of [[Dada]] and [[Surrealism]], Ernst had no formal artistic training. He invented frottage, which uses pencil rubbings of textured surfaces to create images, and grattage, in which paint is scraped across canvas to reveal the imprints of objects beneath. His collage novels repurposed engravings into surreal narratives. He served as a soldier for four years in [[World War I]], an experience that left him critical of the modern world. During World War II he was designated an "undesirable foreigner" while living in France. Ernst often included his alter ego, Loplop, a bird, in his work. He achieved financial success in the 1950s.

German theoretical physicist and originator of quantum theory. He introduced the concept of energy quanta to explain [[Black-body radiation|black-body radiation]]. The [[Planck constant]], h, is of foundational importance for quantum physics, and he used it to derive [[Planck units]], expressed in terms of physical constants. The Planck relation, E = hν, states that the energy of a [[Photon|photon]] is proportional to its frequency. He studied in Berlin with Hermann von Helmholtz and Gustav Kirchhoff, and received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of energy quanta. Twice president of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, he saw it renamed the Max Planck Society in 1948; today it includes 83 institutions.

German philosopher, pen name of Johann Caspar Schmidt. Stirner is best known for *The Ego and Its Own* (1844), which argues for egoism and the sovereignty of the unique individual, dismissing abstractions such as morality, religion and the state. He studied at the University of Berlin, attended the lectures of [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel]] and joined the Young Hegelians. Unable to secure a permanent academic post, he supported himself as a teacher and spent his later years in relative obscurity. Stirner is often seen as a forerunner of [[Nihilism|nihilism]], [[Existentialism|existentialism]] and individualist anarchism. [[Karl Marx]] devoted much of *The German Ideology* to refuting him.

Dutch and Belgian racing driver. He competes in [[Formula One]] for Red Bull Racing and won four consecutive World Drivers' Championships, from 2021 to 2024. In 2021 he overtook [[Lewis Hamilton]] on the final lap of the season's last race to take his first title. As of the 2026 São Paulo Grand Prix he had 74 race wins, 50 pole positions and 139 podiums. His records include the most wins in a season (19) and the most consecutive wins (10). At 18, he became the youngest driver to win a Formula One Grand Prix, at the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix.

German sociologist, historian and jurist. One of the founders of [[Sociology|sociology]], Weber argued in *The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism* that the Protestant work ethic helped shape modern [[Capitalism|capitalism]]. He linked the processes of rationalization and disenchantment to the rise of capitalism and modernity. He defined the state by its monopoly on the legitimate use of force and distinguished three forms of authority: [[Charisma|charismatic]], traditional and rational-legal. He advocated interpretive, rather than purely empiricist, methods for studying social action. He taught in Berlin, Freiburg and Heidelberg. During World War I he became critical of Germany's war effort and supported democratization. After the war he co-founded the German Democratic Party and advised on the Weimar Constitution. His unfinished *Economy and Society* was published posthumously.

Swedish and French actor. He had a 70-year career in European and American film, television and theatre, appearing in more than 150 films. In Ingmar Bergman's *The Seventh Seal* (1957) he played the knight Antonius Block, and he appeared in eleven Bergman films. He made his American film debut as Jesus Christ in *The Greatest Story Ever Told* (1965). He was nominated for two [[Academy Awards]], for Best Actor in *Pelle the Conqueror* (1987) and for Best Supporting Actor in *Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close* (2011). He played Bloodraven in the [[HBO]] series [[Game of Thrones]].

Russian and Soviet writer and proponent of socialism, pen name of Alexei Maximovich Peshkov. His early short stories of the 1890s, marked by romanticism, brought him fame. The play *The Lower Depths* (1902) and the novel *Mother* (1906) followed; Gorky considered the latter one of his biggest failures, though it remains among his best-known books. Active in the Marxist movement, he was associated with [[Vladimir Lenin]] and the [[Bolsheviks]], but he criticized them during the Russian Civil War and the 1920s. He returned to the USSR in 1928 on [[Joseph Stalin]]'s invitation and was declared the "founder of Socialist Realism". His unfinished novel *The Life of Klim Samgin* is considered by some critics his masterpiece. He was nominated five times for the Nobel Prize in Literature and spent his last days under unannounced house arrest.

King of the Romans (1486–1508) and Holy Roman Emperor (1508–1519). Son of Frederick III, he expanded the influence of the [[House of Habsburg]] through war and his 1477 marriage to Mary, Duchess of Burgundy. The journey to Rome was blocked by the [[Venice|Venetians]], so he was never crowned by the pope; he proclaimed himself emperor at Trento in 1508, and [[Pope Julius II]] later recognized it. His son Philip married Joanna of Castile in 1496, helping establish the Habsburg dynasty in [[Spain]]. He lost the family's lands in [[Switzerland]] to the Swiss Confederacy. Historians debate whether he was the "last knight" or a Renaissance prince. He carried out reforms and promoted an extensive image-building program, though his military expansion and financial costs weighed heavily on his subjects.

Austrian archduke and emperor of Mexico (1864–1867). Younger brother of Emperor [[Franz Joseph I]] of Austria, he was invited by [[Napoleon III]] and Mexican monarchists to rule Mexico. He accepted the crown in 1864 after a referendum that purportedly showed popular support. His liberal policies cost him conservative backing. The United States continued to recognize [[Benito Juárez]] and saw the French intervention as a violation of the [[Monroe Doctrine]]. French troops withdrew in 1866. Captured at Querétaro, he was executed by firing squad alongside two generals.
